name: Hannibal
info: Hannibal was a Carthaginian general and statesman who commanded Carthage's forces against the Roman Republic in the Second Punic War, crossed the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE and destroyed a Roman army at Cannae before his defeat at Zama.

facts.born: 247 BCE, most likely in Carthage; son of the Carthaginian general and statesman Hamilcar Barca, whose descendants are known as the Barcids
facts.died: Between 183 and 181 BCE, at Libyssa in Bithynia; according to Cornelius Nepos and Livy he took poison when Roman soldiers surrounded the castle where he lived, though the precise year and cause are unknown
facts.role: Officer under Hasdrubal the Fair in Hispania; commander-in-chief of the Carthaginian army in Iberia from 221 BCE; commander against Rome in the Second Punic War; suffete (chief magistrate) of Carthage after the war; military adviser to Antiochus III and commander for Prusias I of Bithynia
facts.known: The oath never to be a friend of Rome; the crossing of the Alps with war elephants; the victories at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae; fifteen years of war in Italy; the defeat at Zama by Scipio Africanus; financial and political reforms at Carthage; exile and death by poison

t: Hannibal took command of Carthage's army in Iberia at 26, attacked Rome's ally Saguntum and carried the Second Punic War into Italy by crossing the Alps in 218 BCE.
At Cannae in 216 BCE he surrounded and destroyed a larger Roman army, yet he could not take Rome, received little support from Carthage and was worn down over fifteen years in Italy.
Defeated at Zama in 202 BCE, he reformed Carthage's finances as suffete, was driven into exile by his enemies and by Rome, and took poison in Bithynia rather than be surrendered.
dyk: While wintering among the Gauls of northern Italy, Hannibal feared that tribesmen would try to assassinate him to win back Rome's favour, and took to altering his appearance with differently dyed wigs so that they would not recognise him.
ev: After the assassination of Hasdrubal, Hannibal is proclaimed commander-in-chief by the army in Iberia at the age of 26
He leaves New Carthage in late spring, crosses the Pyrenees, the Rhône and the Alps, and enters Italy
He destroys the army of the consul Gaius Flaminius in an ambush on the shore of Lake Trasimene
At Cannae he surrounds a Roman army, of which 50,000–70,000 are estimated killed or captured
He marches on Rome to draw off the besiegers of Capua, but the city falls to the Romans
After nearly 15 years in Italy he is recalled to Carthage to defend it against Scipio Africanus
Scipio defeats him at the Battle of Zama, the last major battle of the Second Punic War
Commanding a Seleucid fleet for Antiochus III, he is forced to retreat by the Rhodian navy at the Battle of Side

sections.early:
Hannibal was born in 247 BCE, most likely in Carthage, one of the sons of the Carthaginian general and statesman Hamilcar Barca; his mother is unknown. He had two brothers, Hasdrubal and Mago, and several sisters whose names are not recorded; his brothers-in-law were Hasdrubal the Fair and the Numidian king Naravas. Barca, meaning "lightning" or "thunderbolt", was a surname his father acquired for the swiftness and ferocity of his attacks.

He grew up in the aftermath of Carthage's defeat by Rome in the First Punic War. Hamilcar set out to restore his family's and Carthage's fortunes by subduing the tribes of the Iberian Peninsula. Carthage was then so poor that it had no navy able to carry his army, and he marched it across Numidia to the Pillars of Hercules. According to Polybius, Hannibal said much later that when he begged to go with his father, Hamilcar agreed and made him swear that he would never be a friend of Rome as long as he lived. One account sets the oath at the age of nine, with Hamilcar holding the boy over a sacrificial fire; tradition places it at Peñíscola.

When Hamilcar drowned in battle, Hannibal's brother-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair succeeded to the command, and Hannibal, then 18, served under him as an officer. Hasdrubal consolidated Carthage's Iberian interests and signed a treaty with Rome by which Carthage would not expand north of the Ebro so long as Rome did not expand south of it. Hannibal's view of military affairs came partly from his Greek tutors and partly from experience gained beside his father.
sections.rise:
On the assassination of Hasdrubal in 221 BCE Hannibal, aged 26, was proclaimed commander-in-chief by the army and confirmed by the Carthaginian government. Livy writes that the old soldiers "fancied they saw Hamilcar in his youth given back to them". Livy also records that he married a woman from Castulo, a powerful Spanish city allied with Carthage.

He spent two years completing the conquest of Hispania south of the Ebro. He stormed Alithia, the strongest centre of the Olcades, and in 220 BCE the Vaccaean strongholds of Helmantice and Arbucala; on the way home he defeated a coalition of tribes led by the Carpetani at the River Tagus, his first major success in the field. Rome, fearing his growing strength, made an alliance with Saguntum, well south of the Ebro. Hannibal took this as a breach of the treaty and, since he was already planning an attack on Rome, besieged the city, which fell after eight months. He sent the booty to Carthage, where, by Livy's record, only Hanno II the Great spoke against him. A Roman delegation led by Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus demanded that Carthage choose between war and peace; told that Rome could choose, Fabius chose war.

Hannibal left New Carthage in late spring 218 BCE and reportedly entered Gaul with 40,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 horsemen. He reached the Rhône by September, with 38 elephants, and evaded a Roman force by turning inland. His route over the Alps has been disputed ever since. According to Polybius, he arrived in Italy with 20,000 foot soldiers, 6,000 horsemen and only a few elephants.
sections.deeds:
Hannibal's appearance in the Po Valley detached the Gauls from Rome. In November 218 BCE his cavalry beat the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio at the Ticinus, a minor victory that brought Gauls and Ligurians to his side and raised his army to around 40,000 men. In December, at the Trebia, he wore down the Roman infantry and then cut it to pieces with an ambush from the flanks. In the spring of 217 BCE he crossed the Apennines and the flooded marshes of the Arno, where he lost a large part of his force and the sight of his right eye. By marching around the consul Gaius Flaminius and cutting him off from Rome he drew him into a defile on the shore of Lake Trasimene and destroyed his army; Flaminius was killed.

In 216 BCE he seized the supply depot at Cannae in Apulia. The Romans raised an army estimated by some at 100,000 men but more likely 50,000–80,000. Hannibal placed his least reliable infantry forward in the centre, let it give way, and closed on the Romans with his Libyan infantry from the wings and his cavalry from behind. It is estimated that 50,000–70,000 Romans were killed or captured, among them the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus and 80 senators.

After Cannae Capua, the second largest city of Italy, came over to him and became his base, and Philip V of Macedon pledged his support. He occupied most of southern Italy for 15 years. In 212 BCE he captured Tarentum and destroyed two Roman armies, with 15,000 and 16,000 Romans killed, and in 208 BCE the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus fell in battle against him.
sections.opponents:
Rome's answer was the strategy of Quintus Fabius Maximus, appointed dictator after Trasimene, who avoided open battle and shadowed Hannibal's army; after Cannae the Romans kept to it, wearing him down with several smaller armies. The Romans refused all overtures for peace and would not ransom the prisoners of Cannae. Only a few of the Italian cities he had hoped to win defected to him, and without siege engines he could not take Rome; his cavalry commander Maharbal is quoted as saying, "Hannibal, you know how to gain a victory, but not how to use one." Capua fell in 211 BCE despite his march on Rome, Tarentum was lost in 209 BCE, and in 207 BCE his brother Hasdrubal was defeated and killed at the Metaurus; his head was thrown into Hannibal's camp.

He was opposed in Carthage too. The peace party of Hanno II the Great, whose wealth rested on trade with Rome, resented the attack on Saguntum as unauthorised and was instrumental in denying him reinforcements after Cannae. Requests for supplies and siege equipment were delayed or ignored.

Most of what is known of him comes from Roman sources. Livy says that he was extremely cruel, and Cicero set the "cruel" Hannibal beside the "honourable" Pyrrhus. Yet he is also recorded as searching for the body of Flaminius and sending the ashes of Marcellus to his family. Polybius, whom some historians judge a partisan witness, says only that the Romans accused him of cruelty and the Carthaginians of avarice, and suggests that he may have been confused with one of his officers, Hannibal Monomachus.
sections.last:
In 203 BCE, after nearly 15 years in Italy, Hannibal was recalled to defend Carthage against a Roman invasion under Scipio Africanus. At Zama the Romans, joined by King Masinissa of Numidia, were superior in cavalry, while Hannibal had more men and 80 war elephants. The Roman cavalry routed the Carthaginian and returned to attack his rear, and his formation collapsed. Carthage lost approximately 20,000 troops, with 15,000 more wounded.

The peace left Carthage with an indemnity of ten thousand talents. Hannibal, 46 at the end of the war in 201 BCE, was elected suffete, the chief magistrate. He reorganised the state finances to eliminate corruption and recover embezzled funds, and had the judges of the Hundred and Four chosen by direct election for a term of one year instead of for life. Seven years after Zama the Romans, alarmed by Carthage's prosperity and suspecting him of contact with Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire, sent a delegation to Carthage. Aware that his reforms had made him many enemies, he fled before his surrender could be demanded.

He went to the court of Antiochus at Ephesus. In 190 BCE, commanding a fleet he had built in Cilicia, he was beaten by the Rhodians at Side. When Antiochus, defeated at Magnesia, promised to hand him over, he fled again, and finally served Prusias I of Bithynia against Eumenes II of Pergamon. The Romans pressed Prusias to give him up. Cornelius Nepos and Livy say that he took poison when soldiers surrounded his house; Pausanias and Appian tell it differently. His death is placed between 183 and 181 BCE.
sections.legacy:
Hannibal became such a figure of terror at Rome that in moments of danger Romans would exclaim "Hannibal ad portas", "Hannibal is at the gates", a phrase still in use. Roman writers such as Livy, Frontinus and Juvenal show a grudging admiration for him, and the Romans are said to have set up statues of him in their streets to advertise the defeat of so worthy an adversary. The historian John Lazenby stresses that Rome's government went on working through the disasters, without revolutions, peace factions or coups, and the war has been called Rome's "finest hour". In the thirteenth century the Byzantine scholar John Tzetzes wrote that Severus, likely Septimius Severus, who was of Libyan birth, built a tomb of white marble for Hannibal at Libyssa.

He is generally regarded as one of the best military strategists and tacticians of all time, and military academies still study his campaigns, above all the double envelopment at Cannae. Alfred von Schlieffen drew on that envelopment in developing his "Schlieffen Plan" before the First World War. Appian tells of a meeting at which Hannibal named Alexander and Pyrrhus as the greatest generals and himself third, adding that had he beaten Scipio he would have put himself before Alexander.

In Tunisia he is widely revered as a national hero: his likeness has appeared on five-dinar notes issued in 1993 and 2013, and a station on the TGM railway line is named Carthage Hannibal. In Turkey a cenotaph was built in his memory in 1981 south of present-day Gebze, as an expression of Atatürk's respect for him.

summary: Hannibal, son of Hamilcar Barca, led a Carthaginian army over the Alps in 218 BCE and defeated Rome at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae, but could not end the war. Beaten at Zama in 202 BCE, he reformed Carthage as suffete, fled into exile and died in Bithynia between 183 and 181 BCE.
references: Dexter Hoyos, Hannibal's dynasty power and politics in the western Mediterranean, 247–183 BC (Routledge, 2003)
Dexter Hoyos, Hannibal : Rome's greatest enemy (Bristol Phoenix Press, 2008)

Adrian Goldsworthy, Cannae: Hannibal's Greatest Victory (Phoenix, 2001)
Simon Hornblower, Hannibal and Scipio: Parallel Lives (Cambridge University Press, 2024)
notes: Era written BCE (the article writes BC), as in the guide's examples.

Death: 'between 183 and 181 BC'; Atticus 183 (Livy implies the same), Polybius 182, Sulpicius Blitho 181. end set to -183, endCirca true. The article says 'the precise year and cause ... are unknown' and gives four accounts (Pausanias: a wounded finger and fever; Nepos and Livy: poison when surrounded; Appian: poisoned by Prusias); the lead states the suicide by poison flatly.

The Hasdrubal who succeeded Hamilcar and was assassinated in 221 BC is called only 'Hasdrubal' in those sentences of the article; I identified him with the brother-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair named earlier in the same section (not the brother Hasdrubal, killed at the Metaurus in 207 BC).
Saguntum: the lead dates the attack to 218 BC; the body gives no year, only an eight-month siege before the Roman embassy and the late-spring 218 departure. I gave no year for the siege.

Army figures differ within the article: 'reportedly entered Gaul with 40,000 foot and 12,000 horsemen'; at the Rhône '38,000 infantry, 8,000 cavalry, and 38 elephants'; in Italy, by Polybius, '20,000 foot soldiers, 6,000 horsemen'. I used the first and the last and the 38 elephants. The article notes that Lancel questions the departure figures.

Loss of the eye: 'he lost his right eye because of conjunctivitis' while crossing the Apennines; I wrote 'the sight of his right eye' and joined it to the Arno marshes. Editor may prefer the article's exact wording.
Cannae: 'the Libyan mercenaries on the wings' in the article; I wrote 'Libyan infantry'. The dead are '50,000–70,000 Romans ... killed or captured'.
'destroyed two Roman armies, with 15,000 and 16,000 Romans killed' in 212 BCE: Silarus (16,000-man army, 15,000 killed) and first Herdonia (18,000 men, 16,000 dead).
Zama: the article says 'Scipio's cavalry attacked Hannibal's rear'; 'returned to attack' is my joining of two sentences. Masinissa 'changed sides in 206 BC'.

Exile year: the heading says 'after 195 BC' and the text 'seven years after the victory of Zama'; no explicit year in the prose, so none is given and the event list skips it. The dates of his suffeteship are given only in a heading (200-196 BC).

Left out as inconsistent: 'In 190 BC he gained a naval victory over Eumenes' with snake-filled pots (placed by the article after the truce of January 189 BC) and 'In 184 BC Hannibal defeated Eumenes two more times'. Also left out: the Armenian stay at Artaxias I's court (Strabo and Plutarch; the Artaxata story is called apocryphal), the flight to Crete, the Alpine route debate in detail, and the vinegar-and-fire rockfall (Livy only).
'Hannibal's house' in 'last' is 'the castle where he was living' in the article; the facts box uses 'castle'.
'the Romans are said to have set up statues': the article states it flatly ('The Romans even built statues of him in the streets of Rome').

Wanted but not in the article: Hamilcar's death year and Hannibal's age at leaving Carthage (only '9 years old' in one account); the year of the suffeteship; the year of the flight; the terms of the final peace of 201 BCE beyond the indemnity; the number of his own losses at Cannae.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
